items.readable_text:
Content:
Given an angle [MATH: \theta] (pronounced "th-ay-ta") in a right triangle, the sides of the triangle have some special names: opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse.

Content:
- Opposite: the side opposite to the angle [MATH: \theta.]
- Adjacent: the side next to (or touching) the angle [MATH: \theta.]
- Hypotenuse: the longest side of the triangle, which is always opposite to the right angle.

Content:
The opposite and adjacent sides are relative to the angle in question. If [MATH: \theta] is representing the other angle, then the name of these sides change to reflect their position relative to the other angle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ffced42dcc71e14b375ec389de911f25]

Content:
Note that the variable [MATH: \theta] is the most commonly used variable in trigonometry, just like [MATH: x] in algebra. However, other variables are often used as well.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given an angle [MATH: \theta] (pronounced "th-ay-ta") in a right triangle, the sides of the triangle have some special names: opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse.

Content:
- Opposite: the side opposite to the angle [MATH: \theta.]
- Adjacent: the side next to (or touching) the angle [MATH: \theta.]
- Hypotenuse: the longest side of the triangle, which is always opposite to the right angle.

Content:
The opposite and adjacent sides are relative to the angle in question. If [MATH: \theta] is representing the other angle, then the name of these sides change to reflect their position relative to the other angle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ffced42dcc71e14b375ec389de911f25]

Content:
Note that the variable [MATH: \theta] is the most commonly used variable in trigonometry, just like [MATH: x] in algebra. However, other variables are often used as well.

---

- the opposite side is [MATH: \overline{MK},]
- the adjacent side is [MATH: \overline{LM},] and
